nicaea-1.title: First Council of Nicaea
nicaea-1.caption: 325 · Nicaea (modern İznik, Turkey)
nicaea-1.alt: Illustration for First Council of Nicaea — Nicaea (modern İznik, Turkey)
nicaea-1.summary: Summoned by Constantine — a still-unbaptized political ruler, with roughly 300 bishops present and the pope sending only legates — the council condemned Arius's teaching that the Son was a created being, affirming him instead as 'begotten, not made, being of one substance (homoousios) with the Father.' It produced the original short creed of 325, ending simply 'And in the Holy Ghost,' and fixed a common method for dating Easter apart from the Passover calendar. Consequence: The homoousios formula became the touchstone test of Trinitarian orthodoxy for essentially every church descending from this council — the Arian controversy, unlike later splits, left no lasting separate communion — and Athanasius, present only as a young deacon, spent his life defending it against Arian resurgence.

constantinople-1.title: First Council of Constantinople
constantinople-1.caption: 381 AD · Constantinople (Church of Hagia Irene)
constantinople-1.alt: Illustration for First Council of Constantinople — Constantinople (Church of Hagia Irene)
constantinople-1.summary: The council expanded the 325 creed into the fuller Niceno-Constantinopolitan form, adding articles on the Holy Spirit, the Church, baptism, and the resurrection, while condemning Apollinarianism and the teaching that the Spirit was a creature. Its Canon 3 also ranked the Bishop of Constantinople second after Rome 'because Constantinople is New Rome' — a promotion for the imperial capital that Rome rejected as never submitted to the Apostolic See. Consequence: The 381 wording is the creed nearly all Christians still recite — but the West's later Filioque addition to it, never accepted in the East, remains a live, unresolved dispute between the Catholic and Protestant West and the Eastern Orthodox churches to this day.

ephesus.title: Council of Ephesus
ephesus.caption: 431 · Ephesus
ephesus.alt: Illustration for Council of Ephesus — Ephesus
ephesus.summary: Opened by Cyril of Alexandria before the bishops sympathetic to Nestorius had even arrived, the council deposed Nestorius, Patriarch of Constantinople, for teaching Christ as two loosely joined persons — declaring him 'excluded from the episcopal dignity, and from all priestly communion.' It endorsed Cyril's letters affirming Mary as Theotokos, 'Mother of God,' against Nestorius's preferred 'Mother of Christ.' Consequence: The Church of the East — the Persian tradition, later called Nestorian — did not accept the condemnation, and 431 is the root of its separation from the rest of the church, the first branch to split off on this site's own family tree.

chalcedon.title: Council of Chalcedon
chalcedon.caption: 451 · Chalcedon (Bithynia, across the Bosphorus from Constantinople; modern Kadıköy, Istanbul)
chalcedon.alt: Illustration for Council of Chalcedon — Chalcedon (Bithynia, across the Bosphorus from Constantinople; modern Kadıköy, Istanbul)
chalcedon.summary: Convened by Emperor Marcian with some 500-520 bishops — the largest of the first seven councils — it condemned Eutyches's one-fused-nature teaching, deposed Dioscorus of Alexandria for the 449 'Robber Synod,' and issued the Chalcedonian Definition: one Person in two natures, 'unconfusedly, immutably, indivisibly, inseparably.' It presented this as continuous with Nicaea, Constantinople, Cyril, and Pope Leo's Tome — not as anything new. Consequence: The Oriental Orthodox communions — Coptic, Ethiopian, Eritrean, Armenian Apostolic, Syriac — rejected the two-natures formula and separated from both Rome and the Byzantine churches in 451, a split still unhealed, though twentieth-century dialogues found substantial underlying agreement on Christ's person.

constantinople-2.title: Second Council of Constantinople
constantinople-2.caption: 553 · Constantinople
constantinople-2.alt: Illustration for Second Council of Constantinople — Constantinople
constantinople-2.summary: Justinian summoned this council to condemn the 'Three Chapters' — the person and writings of Theodore of Mopsuestia, certain writings of Theodoret, and Ibas's letter to Mari — as tending toward Nestorianism, hoping to win the anti-Chalcedonian churches back while still upholding Chalcedon. Pope Vigilius, brought to Constantinople and held there against his will, resisted and then capitulated under imperial pressure in December 553. Consequence: The reconciliation failed on both sides: the Oriental Orthodox did not return to communion, and in the West the condemnation itself touched off the decades-long Three Chapters Schism among Latin churches, notably Aquileia and Milan.

constantinople-3.title: Third Council of Constantinople
constantinople-3.caption: 680-681 AD · Constantinople (Trullus hall, imperial palace)
constantinople-3.alt: Illustration for Third Council of Constantinople — Constantinople (Trullus hall, imperial palace)
constantinople-3.summary: Meeting in the domed hall of the imperial palace under Constantine IV, the council condemned Monothelitism — the politically convenient teaching that Christ had only one will — affirming two natural wills and operations, the human in perfect, non-resistant subjection to the divine. It anathematized by name several past patriarchs and, remarkably, Pope Honorius I of Rome, 'because of what we found written by him to Sergius.' Consequence: Pope Leo II confirmed the decrees — anathema against his predecessor included — and no schism followed, but the condemnation of a dead pope as a heretic became a standing complication cited centuries later in the debates over papal infallibility at Vatican I.

nicaea-2.title: Second Council of Nicaea
nicaea-2.caption: 787 AD · Nicaea (Church of Hagia Sophia, Nicaea, Bithynia)
nicaea-2.alt: Illustration for Second Council of Nicaea — Nicaea (Church of Hagia Sophia, Nicaea, Bithynia)
nicaea-2.summary: Convened by Empress Irene, regent for her minor son — a woman ruler calling an ecumenical council — with roughly 350 bishops and Patriarch Tarasius presiding, it restored the veneration of icons, ending the first period of Byzantine Iconoclasm. Its Definition drew a firm line between latria, worship due to God alone, and the honorable reverence given to images, which passes through the object to the person depicted, not to the wood or paint. Consequence: This ruling is why Orthodox and Catholic churches still venerate icons today — though the settlement did not hold at first: a second Iconoclasm began around 815 and was only reversed in 843, when Empress Theodora restored the icons in what the East still commemorates as the 'Triumph of Orthodoxy.'

trent.title: Council of Trent
trent.caption: 1545–1563 · Trent (Trento, Italy)
trent.alt: Illustration for Council of Trent — Trent (Trento, Italy)
trent.summary: Called and carried forward entirely by popes — the shift from imperial to papal convocation complete — Trent met in 25 sessions across 18 years as the Catholic answer to the Reformation. It declared Scripture and unwritten Tradition received with equal reverence, fixed the Catholic canon including the deuterocanonical books, reaffirmed justification by faith and works together against Luther's sola fide, upheld all seven sacraments, required every diocese to found a seminary, and kept indulgences while ordering their abuses corrected. Consequence: Trent's canon of 46 Old Testament and 27 New Testament books became fixed and binding — closing a question the early Church had never settled by universal council — and its 'equal reverence' for Tradition set Catholic teaching against sola scriptura in a division never since resolved.

vatican-1.title: First Vatican Council
vatican-1.caption: 1869–1870 · Rome (St. Peter's Basilica)
vatican-1.alt: Illustration for First Vatican Council — Rome (St. Peter's Basilica)
vatican-1.summary: The council's fourth session adopted Pastor Aeternus on July 18, 1870, defining papal infallibility: the pope speaking ex cathedra on faith or morals is preserved from error, his definitions 'irreformable of themselves, and not from the consent of the Church.' The vote was 533 to 2 — but some 55-60 opposed bishops left Rome rather than vote no, and two months later Italian troops seized the city, ending the council so abruptly it was not formally closed until 1960. Consequence: The definition remains a principal point of division from the Orthodox and Protestant churches, and a group of mainly German-speaking Catholics — including Döllinger, excommunicated in 1871 — refused it and split off to form the Old Catholic Church.

vatican-2.title: Second Vatican Council
vatican-2.caption: 1962-1965 · St. Peter's Basilica, Vatican City, Rome
vatican-2.alt: Illustration for Second Vatican Council — St. Peter's Basilica, Vatican City, Rome
vatican-2.summary: Framed by John XXIII as aggiornamento — 'bringing up to date' — Vatican II produced sixteen documents across four sessions from 1962 to 1965. It opened the Mass to vernacular languages and restored communion under both kinds to the laity; Nostra Aetate repudiated the charge of collective Jewish guilt for Christ's death and condemned antisemitism; and Gaudium et Spes became the first pastoral constitution by an ecumenical council to address the whole world directly. Consequence: The vernacular liturgy and Nostra Aetate reshaped everyday Catholic worship and Catholic-Jewish relations worldwide — effects still in force — while a traditionalist minority, notably the Society of St. Pius X, rejected the reforms, an internal split that continues.
